description: Whether we are building prosolution or optimizing a predictive model under a tight deadline, I focus on rapid prototyping, clean architecture, and turning raw data into working products.
summary: MarsWalk Navigator is a hyper-local route planner for Mars astronauts. Global tools such as Mars Trek are built for regional views: one pixel of their global mosaics is 232–463 m, larger than our whole 210 m sample walk. We built a web tool that takes a 900 m × 677 m window of Gale Crater boxwork terrain, resamples the USGS MSL Gale DEM to a 3.005 m grid, and runs 8-connected A* between two points chosen by the user. It returns three compared routes: shortest, gentlest slope and a ridge-seeking heuristic. For each route it shows length, ascent, max and mean slope and a ridge score, and the user sets the slope cap. In our reset sample the gentlest route is 5% longer but has about half the peak slope. The tool states its limits openly: no soil traction, rock or sand data, and the ridge score is a terrain heuristic, not a measurement.
details:
What it does. MarsWalk Navigator helps a Mars crew plan one walk. The user picks a start and a destination on a 900 m × 677 m window of Gale Crater boxwork terrain and gets three least-cost routes: shortest, gentlest slope and a ridge-seeking heuristic. Length, ascent, descent, max slope, mean slope and ridge score are shown for each, and the user sets the slope cap.

How it works. The USGS MSL Gale DEM mosaic (labelled 1 m), served through NASA/JPL Mars Trek, was cropped and resampled to a 300 × 225 grid of 3.005 m cells. Slope and a topographic-position “ridge score” are computed per cell. An 8-connected A* search treats cells above the slope cap as walls. Step cost = distance × (1 + slope weight × (slope ÷ cap)²) + ridge weight × distance × (1 − ridge score). The three routes differ only by their weights: 0/0, 12/0 and 1.5/8.

Results. In our reset sample (15° cap) the gentlest route is 221.2 m against 210.6 m for the shortest, 5% longer, with a peak slope of 7.5° instead of 14.7°. In a second sample, 95 m apart with a 27° cap, no route avoids a 26.5° cell. The gentlest route is 12.8% longer but lowers the mean slope by 2.7°.

Why it matters. Global maps show the planet; a walk is smaller than one of their pixels. Our tool works at walking scale and states its limits: no soil traction, rock or sand data; DEM crop resolution not verified; the ridge score is a heuristic, not a measurement; routes are planning examples, not rover commands.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript (web app and A* pathfinder); Python for raster clipping and manifest checks.

Next. Radiation and dust-storm layers, rock hazards, local geology, Curiosity photos at each stop, live rover telemetry.

SI acknowledgement. An AI assistant (Curser) was used to help brainstorm the concept, draft parts of the code, and draft the presentation and this text. The team chose the site and data, ran and checked the calculations, and is responsible for the final work.
